Laboratory incubation trials have provided detailed developmental data for the Spotted-tail salamander (Eurycea lucifuga), revealing how thermal conditions shape early life stages. At a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the embryonic period extended considerably: the age at hatch was recorded as 72.8 days , followed by an age at birth of 106 days [ab = 106 days], marking the completion of yolk absorption. Development accelerated substantially at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], with hatching occurring after 24.6 days  and birth following at approximately 100 days [ab = approximately 100 days]. The warmest treatment, 21 °C [T = 21 °C], yielded the most rapid ontogenetic progression, with hatching at only 18 days  and birth at 74 days [ab = 74 days]. These thermal responses are consistent with the general metabolic sensitivity observed among plethodontid salamanders, although the comparatively slow developmental pace at 10 °C may reflect an adaptation to cool, spring-fed headwater streams.

Alongside the temporal variation in embryonic development, the rate of larval growth during the immediate post-hatching interval also exhibited a clear thermal dependency. The change in total length at birth was measured at three distinct temperatures, providing a metric of early somatic expansion. At 10 °C [T = 10 °C], larvae grew at a rate of 0.05 centimeters per day , reflecting the suppressed metabolic activity characteristic of cooler environments. This rate increased to 0.07 centimeters per day  when individuals were reared at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], and reached a maximum of 0.09 centimeters per day  under incubation at 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. The magnitude of this thermal acceleration, a nearly two-fold increase from the coolest to the warmest treatment, underscores the importance of local hydroperiod and thermal regime in determining recruitment success for this species.

Morphometric analysis of individuals across different life stages has clarified several key size thresholds in the species' ontogeny. Newly hatched larvae, immediately following eclosion, exhibit a total length of 1.2 centimeters , representing the size at which the chorion ruptures and the larva begins its free-swimming, yolk-dependent phase. By the time of yolk absorption, which marks the completion of the lecithotrophic larval stage and the onset of exogenous feeding, individuals have grown to a total length of 1.82 centimeters [Lb = 1.82 centimeters]. This length increment during the yolk-dependent period is critical, as it directly influences the size at which larvae begin foraging and thus their competitive ability in shared aquatic habitats. The ultimate total length attained by adult Spotted-tail salamanders, based on a comprehensive survey of museum specimens and field captures, is 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters], a value that places Eurycea lucifuga among the larger members of its genus.

Sexual maturation in this species appears to occur at a size notably below the ultimate length. Females reach puberty at a total length of 7.8 centimeters [Lp = 7.8 centimeters], a figure derived from a conversion of the reported snout-vent length of 4.8 centimeters using the species-specific body proportion ratio. Males, which are generally slightly smaller upon reaching reproductive maturity, attain puberty at a total length of 7.5 centimeters [Lp = 7.5 centimeters]. This size dimorphism at the onset of gonadal activity is modest but consistent with the pattern observed in other stream-dwelling plethodontids, where females often defer reproduction until a larger body size to accommodate egg production. The maximum wet weight recorded among adult individuals in the study population was 3.7 grams [Wwi = 3.7 grams], although whether this represents the true asymptotic mass or simply the largest individual sampled remains uncertain given the limited sample size of very large animals.

The reproductive schedule of the Spotted-tail salamander is constrained by a relatively low potential output. An analysis of field records and captive observations indicated that females, when maintained at a stable temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], produce one clutch every other year [F_R_i = one clutch every other year], with approximately 17 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 17 eggs per clutch], a slow reproductive pace typical of long-lived amphibians inhabiting stable, low-productivity subterranean or spring-fed environments. This infrequent breeding effort highlights the species' conservative life-history strategy. The species also exhibits a notably extended lifespan, with the oldest documented individual surviving for 9.1 years [am = 9.1 years] under captive conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a longevity that places it among the longer-lived members of the genus. This combination of delayed reproduction and low fecundity positions Eurycea lucifuga as a classic K-selected strategist among North American salamanders, with population dynamics driven primarily by adult survival rather than high recruitment rates.
